stories.headline: Nepal seeks grants, not loans, for flood recovery after deadly glacier disaster
stories.title: Nepal seeks grants, not loans, for flood recovery after deadly glacier disaster
stories.summary: When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega ​loan or a patchwork ‌of small grants, Nepal PM Shah says
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah called for grant-based international support at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday to help the Himalayan nation recover from the glacier flood that killed at least 1,450 people.

Shah said in New York that Nepal’s recovery and reconstruction needs were estimated at about 10 per cent of gross domestic product following the flood that struck mountain communities four weeks ago, and argued that vulnerable countries should not be forced to take on additional debt to rebuild from catastrophic climate events.
“When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants,” Shah said.
“We need adequate grant-based support from the world.”

He urged closer cooperation between Nepal, India and China on climate resilience, calling for an urgent Himalayan mechanism to share satellite data, monitor glacial lakes, strengthen early-warning systems and coordinate disaster responses across borders.

The Nepalese leader said the flood, which he described as a warning of the growing risks posed by climate change, had swept away roads, bridges, schools, homes and livelihoods, interrupting Nepal’s development progress.
The collapse of a glacier near the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet Autonomous Region in late August triggered landslides and a flash flood that tore through valleys downstream.
Weeks later, search and recovery operations were still under way, with more than 6,000 people remaining missing in the area.
Shah said many of them may never be found.
The World Bank earlier this week made available up to $170 million in emergency financing to help Nepal respond to the disaster and begin recovery efforts.

stories.headline: China's Top Producers Agree To Make Less Silicon From October. Should Indian Manufacturers Be Worried?
stories.title: China's Top Producers Agree To Make Less Silicon From October. Should Indian Manufacturers Be Worried?
stories.summary: Ten of China's leading polysilicon producers met in Beijing on September 11 and reportedly agreed to something the industry has talked about, without success, for nearly two years: actually cutting output. Under the terms of the agreement, circulating in a document cited by Bernreuter Research, each company would cap its utilisation rate at 35 per cent of nameplate capacity, equivalent to a combined 1.028 million tonnes, with monthly production and sales limits of 85,700 tonnes apiece. If implemented from October as planned, the caps would hold 2026 output to roughly 1.144 million tonnes against expected demand of about 1.2 million tonnes, the first time in years that Chinese supply would run below what the market demand. History gives us good reason to be skeptical. Identical caps applied uniformly across companies with very different plant ages and cost structures have a poor record of surviving contact with individual producers' balance sheets. But the timing matters regardless of whether October's caps stick to the letter. China's dominant polysilicon makers, who supply roughly 90 per cent of the world's raw silicon for solar cells, have spent the past two years dumping inventory at prices well below production cost as capacity additions outran demand. Daqo New Energy, one of the biggest and more disciplined producers, watched its own average selling price fall as n-type polysilicon dropped from the RMB 48-55 per kg range at the end of 2025 to the RMB 31-34 per kg range by mid-2026, against a production cost of nearly RMB 43 per kg. That collapse is precisely what October's caps are designed to reverse. Two Years of Cheap Inputs, Ending For India's solar manufacturing sector, two years of collapsing polysilicon prices have been a quiet subsidy. Even as the ALMM list and Domestic Content Requirement rules pushed Indian module makers to source cells domestically, the wafers and cells feeding much of that capacity, and the raw polysilicon behind the parts not yet made locally, have ridden China's oversupply down to some of the cheapest levels in the industry's history. That subsidy could now be ending. Which will be tough on customers, as despite all the low input costs, Indian module prices have stayed stubbornly at a 100% or more premium to Chinese prices. “For two years Indian manufacturers built capacity against a falling cost curve. Whether they benefit or get squeezed depends on whether their own plants are running before China's caps bite.” Testing India's Timing India has added over 55 GW of module and 13 GW of cell manufacturing capacity so far in 2026, according to MNRE data and comoany announcements, with the top ten manufacturers now accounting for close to 64 per cent of total module capacity. A wave of backward-integration projects, from Vikram Solar's 9 GW cell facility due in FY2027, ReNew's planned 6.5 GW ingot-wafer plant in Andhra Pradesh, and Solarworld Energy's 2.4 GW cell joint venture with Rays Power among them, are explicitly aimed at reducing exposure to exactly this kind of external price swing. Most of that capacity, however, is still ramping rather than running, and India's near-term project pipeline will depend on imported wafers from China's spot market. If October's utilisation caps hold even partially, the input costs feeding that pipeline could start rising just as several of India's own wafer and cell plants are still months from commissioning, a timing gap that could pressure margins on projects bid at today's tariffs but built using tomorrow's, likely higher, input costs. Conversely, if Indian capacity comes online broadly on schedule through FY2027, tighter Chinese supply could offer some protection from being accused of high prices under the protection of tariff and non tariff barriers. Something that has plagued the industry till now for cell making.

stories.title: Nepal PM proposes Himalayan climate resilience mechanism with India, China
stories.summary: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah has proposed establishing a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by his country as well as India and China, in the wake of the recent devastating flash floods in the area.
